title: The Saint Michael prayer (1886)
hook: Leo XIII's prayer for protection, once said after every Mass

segments.voice: Yesterday, medals and scapulars: reminders you can touch, never a password. Your line was not a charm. What did yours remind you of? Day one thousand three hundred eighty.

There was a time when a quiet Mass ended differently. The priest finished, and nobody left. He knelt at the foot of the altar, the people knelt with him, and together they prayed a few more prayers aloud. One of them wasn't addressed to God the Father, or to Mary. It was addressed to an angel, and it began by asking him to defend us in battle. Some parishes have started saying it again after Mass. Today: that prayer, and the angel it calls on.
screen: `NOBODY LEFT.` → `A FEW MORE PRAYERS, KNEELING.` → `ONE OF THEM: TO AN ANGEL.`

segments.voice: Start with the angel. The Apocalypse says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And there was a great battle in heaven, Michael and his angels fought with the dragon." In the book of Daniel, Michael is a great prince who stands up for his people. Scripture gives him the role of protector. Next, the pope. Pope Leo the Thirteenth wrote a short prayer to Michael in Latin and added it to the prayers said kneeling at the end of Low Mass. A story people tell says he wrote it after a frightening vision during Mass. There's no firm record of that, and the prayer doesn't need it. When the liturgy was reformed after the Second Vatican Council, those prayers at the end of Mass were dropped. The Saint Michael prayer itself stayed in Catholic life. Pope John Paul the Second later urged Catholics to pray it, and some parishes have brought it back. Third, what it asks. It asks Michael to defend us in battle and to be a protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil. It asks God, humbly, to rebuke him. And it asks Michael, by the power of God, to drive Satan and the evil spirits who roam the world back into hell. Strong words. But notice the order: even the warrior angel acts by God's power, not his own. Fourth, which battle. Paul writes to the Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims: "For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood." Not against the coworker, the ex, the neighbor with the barking dog, the people on the other side of an argument. Whatever this prayer is fighting, it's never a person. That's worth remembering each time someone says defend us in battle.
screen: `MICHAEL FOUGHT THE DRAGON.` · `LEO THE THIRTEENTH, AFTER LOW MASS.` · `BY THE POWER OF GOD.` · `NOT AGAINST FLESH AND BLOOD.` · then, large: `DEFEND US IN BATTLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray it once, or sit with its first request. Take one long breath. If you know the Saint Michael prayer, or have it on a card, and you pray, you can say it once, slowly. If you don't know it, stay with the opening words: defend us in battle. Bring to mind one struggle you're in right now. Then do the hard part. Separate the struggle from the people in it. Let anyone you've been treating as the enemy step out of the frame. What's left is the real fight. Breathe there. The bell holds the time.
The Saint Michael prayer. Pope Leo the Thirteenth's short prayer asking the archangel to defend us in battle, once said at the end of Low Mass, still prayed by some Catholics today. Today's word.

Your line: defend us in battle. Today, when you feel a fight rising with someone, remember Paul: not against flesh and blood. Aim at the problem, not the person. Day one thousand three hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Some Catholics pray the Saint Michael prayer daily, and some parishes say it together at the end of Mass; it asks the archangel's protection against evil.

original.note: Latin: defend us in battle. Leo XIII wrote the prayer in Latin; it opens Sancte Michael Archangele, defende nos in proelio.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer for winning fights.
what it means: a plea for protection against evil, made by God's power, never aimed at a person.
what a scholar hears: Leo XIII added it to the prayers after Low Mass; those prayers were dropped in the liturgical reform, and the story of his vision has no firm source.

notes: The prayer is described, not quoted, from the Latin (Sancte Michael Archangele, defende nos in proelio; contra nequitiam et insidias diaboli esto praesidium...). 'Defend us in battle' is the index carry. Confirm the description.

Leo XIII composed the prayer and added it to the Leonine prayers after Low Mass (the title gives 1886); no date is stated in the voice. The prayers after Low Mass were suppressed in the liturgical reform (1964 instruction Inter Oecumenici). Confirm.
The vision story is labeled 'a story people tell' with 'no firm record'; confirm this is fair.
John Paul II urged Catholics to pray it (Regina Caeli, 24 April 1994); confirm. 'Some parishes have brought it back' is a general observation.
Day 1031 covered the three archangels and Michael's name; this day avoids the name's meaning and Jude 9.
Douay-Rheims wording of Apocalypse 12:7 and Ephesians 6:12: confirm.

Editor pass: hook no longer says the Michael prayer was the last of the prayers after Low Mass (an invocation of the Sacred Heart was later added after it); cut a repeated 'never a person' line; varied the practice's settling line.
